concepts.name: The membership question
concepts.summary: Programs often need to know whether they have seen an item before. An exact set answers this but stores every item, so its memory grows with the items themselves. A Bloom filter trades a little exactness for a fixed, small cost of a few bits per item, however long each item is.

misconceptions.description: Thinks a Bloom filter stores the items; it only stores bits.

concepts.name: Hash functions as scatter
concepts.summary: A hash function maps any input to a number: the same input always gives the same number, and different inputs spread evenly over the range. A Bloom filter needs k positions per item. Double hashing derives them from two base hashes as (h1 + i * h2) mod m, which in practice works almost as well as k independent hash functions.

misconceptions.description: Thinks a hash can give a different answer for the same input; it is deterministic.

concepts.name: Insert and query
concepts.summary: A Bloom filter is m bits, all 0 at first, and k hash functions. Inserting an item sets its k bits to 1. A query checks the same k bits: if any is 0 the item was definitely never inserted; if all are 1 it was probably inserted. There are no false negatives, because inserting an item sets every bit a later query for it will check.

misconceptions.description: Thinks a Bloom filter can miss an item that was inserted; it cannot.

concepts.name: False positives
concepts.summary: A query answers probably yes wrongly when other items happened to set all k of its bits. After n inserts into m bits with k hashes, a given bit is still 0 with probability about e^(-kn/m), so the false-positive rate is about (1 - e^(-kn/m))^k. The rate rises as the filter fills.

misconceptions.description: Thinks the false-positive rate is fixed; it rises as more items are added.

concepts.name: Choosing k and m
concepts.summary: More hash functions check more bits per query but also set more bits per insert. For given m and n the rate is lowest at k = (m/n) ln 2, which leaves about half the bits set, and the rate is then about 0.6185^(m/n). To hold n items at rate p you need about m = -n ln p / (ln 2)^2 bits: roughly 9.6 bits per item for 1%.

sources.label: Choosing The Number Of Hashes And Bits

misconceptions.description: Thinks more hash functions always lower the rate; past the optimum they raise it.

concepts.name: Deletion and counting filters
concepts.summary: Clearing an item's bits could clear bits that other items rely on, which would create false negatives, so a plain Bloom filter cannot delete. A counting Bloom filter keeps a small counter per position instead of a bit: insert increments, delete decrements. It supports deletion at the cost of several times more memory.

misconceptions.description: Thinks you can delete by clearing the item's k bits.
